title: Magnetic-Field-Induced Darkening of Bright Excitons in a MoWSe$_2$ Monolayer Alloy
authors: Katarzyna Olkowska-Pucko, Artur O. Slobodeniuk, Mehdi Arfaoui, Elena Blundo, Natalia Zawadzka, Łucja Kipczak, Jan Szpakowski, Diana Vaclavkova, Dipankar Jana, Piotr Kapuściński, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Clement Faugeras, Marek Potemski, Adam Babiński, Antonio Polimeni, Maciej R. Molas
abstract: Magnetic fields are widely used to brighten spin-forbidden dark excitons, but the inverse effect on an optically bright exciton has remained largely unexplored. We demonstrate the complementary phenomenon of magnetic-field-induced darkening of a bright exciton in Mo$_{0.68}$W$_{0.32}$Se$_2$. At 4.2 K, an in-plane magnetic field up to 25 T activates a dark-exciton line 14.2$\pm$1.3 meV below the bright exciton while suppressing the bright-exciton emission by about 85\%. A bright-dark mixing model quantitatively captures the coupled energy and intensity evolution with an effective in-plane $g$ factor of $|g_{\parallel}|=5.2\pm0.2$. Alloying is crucial to the effect, as it brings the system close to the bright-dark crossover, where a small bright-dark splitting is combined with unusually strong in-plane magnetic coupling. This places the system in a regime where field-induced level repulsion raises the bright-like branch and strongly depletes its thermal population. These results identify a general route to magnetic control of exciton populations through engineering of the bright-dark hierarchy.
summary: This study reports on the magnetic-field-induced darkening of bright excitons in $	ext{Mo}_{0.68}	ext{W}_{0.32}	ext{Se}_2$. By applying an in-plane magnetic field, the bright exciton emission is suppressed by about 85% while a dark exciton state is activated. The findings confirm that alloying is key to enhancing this magnetic control mechanism, offering a general route for manipulating exciton populations.
main_problem: The study investigates the inverse effect of magnetic fields on excitons: the magnetic-field-induced darkening (quenching) of an optically bright exciton, complementing the known brightening of dark excitons.
main_result: The research demonstrates that applying an in-plane magnetic field up to 25 T causes an 85% suppression of bright exciton emission while simultaneously activating a dark exciton line in the $	ext{Mo}_{0.68}	ext{W}_{0.32}	ext{Se}_2$ alloy.
method: The work combines low-temperature photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy with theoretical modeling using a k.p approach and a bright-dark exciton mixing Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{Mo}_{0.68}	ext{W}_{0.32}	ext{Se}_2$ monolayer alloy. The theoretical framework uses a coupled bright-dark exciton mixing model, whose energy and population dynamics are governed by the magnetic field via the Zeeman interaction.
key_observables: Bright-dark splitting ($\Delta$), the magnitude of bright exciton suppression ($\approx 85\%$), and the effective in-plane g factor ($|g_{\parallel}| = 5.2 \pm 0.2$).
important_parameters: Temperature (4.2 K), Magnetic Field ($B_{\parallel}$ up to 25 T), and the alloy composition ($	ext{Mo}_{0.68}	ext{W}_{0.32}	ext{Se}_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes thermal equilibrium and that the alloying brings the system near the bright-dark crossover, enhancing magnetic coupling effects.
figures_summary: Figures show the PL spectra evolution, the quadratic increase of the dark exciton intensity with $B_{\parallel}$, and theoretical fits demonstrating the energy shifts and population quenching based on the mixing model.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting bright/dark exciton behavior, develops a k.p model for coupled energy/intensity evolution, presents experimental PL measurements showing quenching and activation, and concludes by attributing the effect to alloy-enhanced magnetic coupling.
why_interesting: This work provides a clear, tunable mechanism for controlling exciton populations using external fields, which is highly relevant for designing quantum emitters and optical switches in 2D materials.
